verdicts.text: A core infrastructure stack containing a VPC could be managed by Terraform while the application stack is managed by Pulumi and consumes its outputs.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi-terraform README (base64-decoded) says: "The Terraform resource provider for Pulumi lets you consume the outputs contained in Terraform state files from your Pulumi programs." So a Terraform-managed core/VPC stack whose outputs a Pulumi app stack reads is a supported pattern. One caveat: the sample at L52-54 reads the "could be Terraform" core stack through `pulumi.StackReference`, which only reads Pulumi stacks. And `terraform.state.S3Reference` doesn't look like the actual API, which I believe is `RemoteStateReference` (not confirmed because of a GitHub rate limit).
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim is true as a concept, but the code sample next to it doesn't show it working: a Terraform core stack can't be read through StackReference, and `terraform.state.S3Reference` probably isn't a real class.

verdicts.text: `new pulumi.StackReference("core-infra")` with `getOutput("vpcId")` retrieves the `vpcId` output from another Pulumi stack named `core-infra` (StackReference name given without org/project qualification).
verdicts.evidence: `new pulumi.StackReference(name)` plus `.getOutput("vpcId")` is a real API. But a bare name like `"core-infra"` only resolves to a stack called core-infra inside the current org and project. stacks.md L55-60 shows `dev` as shorthand for `my-org/my-project/dev`, and L618 says "Stack names must be fully qualified... in the format `<organization>/<project>/<stack>`". A core-infra stack in a separate project would not be found. The snippet's core stack also exports `vpc`, not `vpcId`, so `getOutput("vpcId")` would come back undefined.
verdicts.framing_note: The API use is valid, but calling core-infra "another Pulumi stack" implies a stack in another project. The bare name only resolves within the current project, and the docs say to use fully qualified names.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The example exports `vpc` but reads `getOutput("vpcId")`, and uses an unqualified stack name where the docs require `org/project/stack`.

verdicts.text: The `@pulumi/terraform` package exposes a `terraform.state.S3Reference` class that takes `bucket` and `key` arguments to reference a Terraform state stored in S3 (also referenced as `pulumi.terraform.state.S3Reference` in the Automation API example).
verdicts.evidence: The generated `@pulumi/terraform` Node.js SDK (sdk/nodejs/state/index.ts on master) has no `S3Reference` class. The `state` module only exports invoke functions: `export const getS3Reference ...`, `getS3ReferenceOutput`, plus getLocalReference, getRemoteReference and getAzureRMReference. So `new terraform.state.S3Reference(...)` with `.getOutput()` isn't a real API. `pulumi.terraform.state.S3Reference` also doesn't exist, because the Terraform state module isn't part of `@pulumi/pulumi`.
verdicts.framing_note: The real API is the function terraform.state.getS3Reference / getS3ReferenceOutput({bucket, key, ...}). It is not a class used with `new`.

verdicts.text: `terraform.state.S3Reference` instances expose a `getOutput(name)` method that returns the named output from the referenced Terraform state.
verdicts.evidence: The Node.js SDK's `sdk/nodejs/state/` directory has only `getAzureRMReference.ts`, `getLocalReference.ts`, `getRemoteReference.ts`, `getS3Reference.ts` and `index.ts`. There is no `S3Reference` class and no `getOutput` method. S3 state is read through an invoke function, `export function getS3Reference(args: GetS3ReferenceArgs, ...): Promise<GetS3ReferenceResult>`, and its result has only `readonly outputs: {[key: string]: any};`. Code should use `terraform.state.getS3ReferenceOutput({...}).outputs["name"]`, not `new S3Reference(...).getOutput(name)`.
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/pulumi-terraform/contents/sdk/nodejs/state/getS3Reference.ts (and directory listing of sdk/nodejs/state)
verdicts.intuition_flag: The PR's code samples seem to borrow the `StackReference.getOutput` pattern for an API that doesn't exist. They also use `pulumi.terraform.state.S3Reference`, which isn't a real namespace either.

verdicts.text: `pulumi import` can be used to bring Terraform-managed resources under Pulumi management.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated CLI reference for `pulumi import` lists the flag "--from string  Invoke a converter to import the resources". verdicts.text: State ownership can be transferred from Terraform to Pulumi gradually, resource-by-resource, during migration.
verdicts.evidence: `pulumi import` adopts individual existing resources by ID, and it "does not modify the actual cloud resource, it only adds the resource to Pulumi's state". Pulumi's migration guide also documents coexisting with Terraform-managed resources by referencing a .tfstate file, so a gradual, per-resource handoff is supported. One third-party guide (Encore) advises running `terraform state rm` after each import and splitting ownership at module boundaries for safety. That is a best-practice caveat, not a limit on what the tools can do.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Pulumi can't take ownership away from Terraform by itself. The user also has to run `terraform state rm` on each resource, and the doc line doesn't say so.

verdicts.text: Pulumi policies (Policy as Code / CrossGuard) can implement infrastructure policies that work across both Terraform and Pulumi resources.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi Policies docs say: "apply them consistently across resources managed by Pulumi IaC, provisioned with Terraform or CloudFormation, or created manually." Coverage of Terraform-provisioned resources comes from audit mode ("Continuously scans resources discovered through Insights Discovery ... including resources created with Terraform"). It does not come from preventative checks during preview or up, which only validate Pulumi stack resources. The example code on the page under review is a preventative policy (a `mandatory` rule checking `aws.ec2.Instance` resources), so on its own it would only check Pulumi-managed resources.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim is broadly true, but only through audit policies on resources found by Insights Discovery (Pulumi Cloud only). The example next to it is a preventative policy, which could lead readers to think it enforces rules on Terraform resources.

verdicts.text: The `@pulumi/policy` package exports `PolicyPack` and `validateResourceOfType`; a policy pack's policies take `name`, `description`, `enforcementLevel: "mandatory"`, and `validateResource` with callback signature `(resource, args, reportViolation)`.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi-policy SDK source has a docstring example that is nearly identical to the doc snippet: `import { PolicyPack, validateResourceOfType } from "@pulumi/policy"; ... enforcementLevel: "mandatory", validateResource: validateResourceOfType(aws.s3.Bucket, (bucket, args, reportViolation) => {`. The `Policy` interface also defines `name`, `description`, and `enforcementLevel`, and `"mandatory"` is one of the allowed `EnforcementLevel` values. One nuance: a plain `validateResource` callback takes `(args, reportViolation)`. The 3-argument `(resource, args, reportViolation)` form is the callback passed to `validateResourceOfType`, which is how the doc uses it.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim attributes the 3-argument signature to `validateResource`, but it actually belongs to the `validateResourceOfType` callback. The doc code itself is correct.

verdicts.text: The `aws.s3.Bucket` resource has an `acl` property that can be `"public-read"` or `"public-read-write"`, and a policy can read it to block public buckets.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi-aws Node.js SDK's `aws.s3.Bucket` has an `acl` property: "Valid values are `private`, `public-read`, `public-read-write`, `aws-exec-read`, `authenticated-read`, and `log-delivery-write`." Because it is a regular resource input, a policy can read it. One caveat: the property is marked "@deprecated acl is deprecated. Use the aws.s3.BucketAcl resource instead."
verdicts.framing_note: The claim names two of the six valid canned-ACL values. The SDK source lists all six, so it covers the claim.
verdicts.intuition_flag: `acl` on aws.s3.Bucket is deprecated in favor of aws.s3.BucketAcl. A policy that only checks Bucket.acl will miss ACLs set through BucketAcl.

verdicts.text: Component resources can wrap Terraform-state-backed infrastructure so that developers create components in Pulumi without knowing they depend on Terraform-managed resources, leaving multi-tool complexity to the platform team.
verdicts.evidence: This pattern works. The pulumi-terraform Node SDK ships Terraform state readers (`sdk/nodejs/state/getS3Reference.ts`, `getRemoteReference.ts`, `getLocalReference.ts`, `getAzureRMReference.ts`). A ComponentResource can call them internally, so consumers of the component never see the Terraform dependency. The multi-tool-complexity benefit is the page's own framing, not a checkable fact.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The sample code near L248/L265 uses `terraform.state.S3Reference` with `.getOutput()`. The current SDK exposes `getS3Reference` as a function rather than that class, so the sample may be out of date.

verdicts.text: Custom component resources extend `pulumi.ComponentResource` and call `super("custom:WebApplication", name, {}, opts)` with a type token, and register outputs via `this.registerOutputs`.
verdicts.evidence: This matches the Node.js SDK (`sdk/nodejs/resource.ts`). There, `ComponentResource` takes a constructor `(type: string, name: string, args?: Inputs, opts?: ComponentResourceOptions)`, and subclasses call the protected `registerOutputs(outputs?)`. So `super("custom:WebApplication", name, {}, opts)` followed by `this.registerOutputs(...)` is the correct pattern. The file I fetched was cut off before the ComponentResource class, so I couldn't quote that part directly.
